what_its_for: Edoxaban is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used to lower your risk of stroke and dangerous blood clots. It is used in people who have an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation (AFib) that is not caused by a heart valve problem. It is also used to treat blood clots in the legs (deep vein thrombosis, or DVT) and lungs (pulmonary embolism, or PE), and to prevent these clots from coming back.
how_to_take: Take edoxaban by mouth exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. If you have trouble swallowing, you may crush the tablet and mix it with 2 to 3 tablespoons of water or applesauce and take it right away. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel fine. Stopping suddenly can increase your risk of dangerous blood clots or stroke.
dosing: The usual dose for most adults is 60 mg once daily. However, your doctor may lower your dose to 30 mg once daily if you have kidney problems, weigh 132 pounds (60 kg) or less, or take certain other medicines. Your doctor will choose the right dose for you. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store edoxaban at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you no longer need the medicine, ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory pain relievers) unless your doctor says it is okay, as these can increase your risk of bleeding. Avoid activities that could cause injury or lead to bleeding, such as contact sports. Limit or avoid alcohol, as it can increase your bleeding risk. Do not start any new prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements (especially St. John's Wort) without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first, as many medicines can interact with edoxaban.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any signs of serious bleeding, such as: unusual bruising, pink, red, or dark brown urine, red or black stools (tarry-looking), coughing or vomiting up blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, heavy or uncontrolled bleeding from a cut, unusual pain or swelling. Also call your doctor if you have a fall, head injury, or any accident. Seek emergency help immediately if you have sudden severe headache, weakness on one side of your body, vision changes, or difficulty speaking, as these could be signs of a stroke or bleeding in the brain.
when_it_works: Edoxaban starts working to thin your blood within 1 to 2 hours after you take your first dose. However, it is important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even when you feel well. This medicine works best when taken consistently at the same time each day.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. If your kidneys do not work well, your dose may need to be lowered or this medicine may not be recommended. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine can cause bleeding problems in an unborn baby and is not recommended during pregnancy. It is not known if it passes into breast milk, so discuss risks with your doctor. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to bleeding side effects and should be monitored closely. Children: This medicine has not been approved for use in children under 18 years of age.
